passage: In the Lisbon school courtyard, Bao waved a phone. "Everyone's going to the rally on Saturday. Share this post so people know you're with us." Ines read the fierce words twice. Some of the phrases Ines did not understand at all. A tug of belonging pulled hard; all the friends had already shared it. "What does it say exactly?" Ines asked. "Just share, it's obvious." Ines frowned. "If it's obvious, you can explain it." Bao's face tightened. Ines put the phone down. "I'll come to hear what the rally is about. But I won't share until I understand it." Bao turned away, then muttered, "Fine."

qa.q: What was Ines feeling about the pressure, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ines felt torn between belonging and not understanding; the hard tug of belonging and the request to explain what the words meant show it.

qa.q: What could Ines do before deciding about sharing?
qa.a: Read the post carefully, ask questions, look for other sources or talk to a trusted adult, and only then decide.

qa.q: How might Bao feel about Ines's answer?
qa.a: Bao may feel hurt or worried about Ines drifting away, as the tightened face suggests; the muttered "Fine" shows some acceptance.

grounding: Friends push Ines to share something fierce and join a rally; Ines chooses to understand first and refuses to share.

Monday. Francis and the others were buzzing about the college fee rally on Saturday. "You're coming, Arnab. Everyone's coming." Francis shoved his phone at him: a fierce poster calling the principal a thief. "Share it on your story."

Arnab didn't know what the fee rise was, or whether the principal had anything to do with it. He felt his stomach knot. Saying no felt like leaving the group. He mumbled, "Later."

Wednesday. He went to the notice board and read the actual fee circular. Then he asked his cousin, who was in college, what was happening. The rise was real, but it came from the state, not the principal. The poster was simply wrong about him.

Friday. Francis asked again. "So, sharing or not?"

"Not that poster. It blames the wrong person," Arnab said. "I'll come to the students' meeting on Monday where they explain the fee thing. If I agree after that, I'll come to the next rally."

Francis rolled his eyes. "You're so slow." But he didn't leave the lunch table.

qa.q: What did the poster call the principal?
qa.a: The poster called the principal a thief.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when Francis pushed him to share the poster?
qa.a: Arnab felt anxious, his stomach knotting, afraid that saying no would mean leaving the group.

qa.q: What did Arnab do that was wise before deciding?
qa.a: Arnab read the actual fee circular and asked his cousin, so he understood the issue before sharing or marching.

qa.q: How does Francis react to Arnab's choice?
qa.a: Francis is impatient and calls Arnab slow, but stays at the lunch table, so the friendship survives.

grounding: It shows a teen pushed by friends to share a fierce post and join a rally he does not fully understand, choosing to understand first rather than act only to belong.

passage:
Santosh, your friends are asking you to march for something you don't understand? Sit. Your Lakshmi Ammamma has a story from her college days.

It was 1979, I was seventeen, in Madurai. All my friends were joining a rally. Big slogans, big banners. My best friend, Selvi, said, "If you don't come, you're against us." I didn't even know what the rally was about, only that everyone was shouting.

I loved those friends. I wanted to stand with them so much my chest ached. But I didn't understand the demand. So I asked my history lecturer to explain both sides. I read the pamphlets from both groups at the library.

In the end I didn't go. I didn't agree with half of what they were demanding. Selvi didn't talk to me for a week.

Then she came back. She said, "At least you know why you didn't come. Half of us didn't know why we did."

Understanding first, Santosh. Belonging will wait for you.

qa.q: Where was Lakshmi Ammamma studying in 1979?
What was young Lakshmi feeling when Selvi pushed her to come?
qa.a: She felt a strong ache to belong with her friends, but also unsure because she did not understand the demand.

qa.q: What choice inside the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Asking her history lecturer and reading both groups' pamphlets mattered most, because it let her decide from understanding rather than pressure.
Selvi realised many of the marchers had joined without knowing why, and respected that Lakshmi had thought it through.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling friends pushing her to join a rally she did not understand, and choosing to understand first rather than act just to belong.
